opus-5.5.text:
I think the advertised number is really a statement about what the model can technically accept as input, not about what it can actually do with that input. You can feed a model a million tokens, and it won't throw an error, but that's a very different thing from saying it can reason over those million tokens the way a person who had carefully read the whole thing could.

A lot of the benchmarks that get used to justify these context lengths are things like needle-in-a-haystack tests, where you hide a single fact somewhere in a long document and ask the model to retrieve it. Models have gotten very good at that, but it's close to the easiest possible long-context task. It's basically a lookup. What's much harder, and much more representative of what we'd actually want from long context, is synthesis: tracking how a character's motivations shift across a novel, noticing that something on page 40 contradicts something on page 300, or understanding a large codebase well enough to make a change that respects constraints scattered across dozens of files. When you test models on that kind of thing, performance tends to degrade well before you hit the nominal limit, sometimes quite sharply.

There's also a training issue. Models see relatively little data where genuinely long-range dependencies matter, and the reinforcement learning or fine-tuning they get mostly involves shorter tasks. So even if the architecture can attend over a long window, the model hasn't necessarily learned to use that capacity well. In my view, the effective context length, meaning the length over which the model can actually do useful work, is often a small fraction of the advertised one.

And I think this matters a lot for forecasting. If you look at what humans do in real jobs, much of it depends on accumulating context over weeks or months: knowing the history of a project, the people involved, the things that were tried and failed. If models can't really hold and integrate that kind of information, that's a significant bottleneck on automating a lot of work, even if they look very impressive on short, self-contained tasks.

r001.rationale: The response says performance degrades well before the nominal limit, sometimes quite sharply.

r002.rationale: It describes needle-in-a-haystack tests as hiding a single fact in a long document and asking the model to retrieve it, calling this close to a lookup.

r003.rationale: It does not propose measuring hallucinations about a supplied long document.

r004.rationale: It proposes testing synthesis across a long text, including tracking changing motivations and detecting contradictions between distant pages.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the simplest way to put it is that the context window is a statement about what the model can technically be fed, not about what it can actually do with what it's fed. So when a lab says a model has a million tokens of context, what that really means is that the architecture and the serving infrastructure won't error out if you give it a million tokens. It says almost nothing about whether the model can retrieve information from the middle of that text, whether it can synthesize across different parts of it, or whether its performance degrades the further you get from the beginning or the end.

And in practice, the degradation is pretty severe. If you look at the evaluations that have been done, the "needle in a haystack" style tests where you insert a single fact somewhere in a very long document and ask the model to find it, models tend to do reasonably well on those. But that's a very easy task. The much harder tasks are ones where you need to hold many pieces of information in mind at once and reason about how they relate to each other. There, models fall off much more quickly, often well before you reach the advertised limit. So the effective context, in the sense of the length over which the model behaves roughly as well as it does on short inputs, is often a small fraction of the nominal window.

Part of the reason is just how these models are trained. The vast majority of the training data consists of relatively short documents, so the model sees very few examples of genuinely long-range dependencies during pretraining. Labs then do some long-context fine-tuning afterwards, but that's a comparatively small amount of data, and it's hard to construct training signals that really require the model to use information from a hundred thousand tokens back. So you end up with a model that has the mechanical capacity to attend over a long sequence but hasn't really learned the skill of doing so.

There's also an incentive problem. Context window size is a very legible number. It's easy to put on a marketing page, and it's easy for customers to compare across providers. Whereas "how well does the model actually use long inputs" is a messy, multidimensional thing that depends on the task, and there's no agreed-upon benchmark that captures it. So the number that gets advertised is the one that's easy to measure and easy to inflate, and the thing that actually matters to users is the one that's hard to measure. That's a fairly common pattern with capability claims more generally, and I think context length is just an unusually clear example of it.

r001.rationale: It says performance degrades severely and often falls off well before the advertised context limit.

r002.rationale: It describes needle-in-a-haystack tests as finding a single inserted fact, then distinguishes that retrieval task from harder long-context reasoning.

r003.rationale: It does not propose measuring hallucinations about a supplied long document.

r004.rationale: It contrasts simple retrieval with tasks requiring the model to relate information across different parts of a long text.

astra-6.text:
Well, the context-window size tells you how much text you can put into the model, but it doesn’t tell you how effectively the model can use that text. Those are quite different things. You might be able to feed in a million tokens, but that doesn’t mean the model can reason about all of them as well as it can reason about a short passage.

For example, one way people test long-context performance is to hide a particular fact in a large document and ask the model to retrieve it. And that’s useful, but it’s a relatively narrow capability. Finding one fact is different from combining evidence scattered across a document, keeping track of how different claims relate to each other, or noticing a contradiction between two distant passages.

So you really want to ask: as you make the context longer, how does performance change on the task you actually care about? Does adding more information help, or does the model start getting distracted and missing things? The advertised window is a limit on the input size. It’s not a guarantee about the quality of the understanding.

r001.rationale: The response says performance may worsen as context grows, but it does not clearly state that degradation within the advertised limit can be substantial.

r002.rationale: It describes hiding a fact in a large document and retrieving it, then distinguishes that narrow test from general long-context understanding.

r003.rationale: It does not propose evaluating hallucinations about a supplied long document.

r004.rationale: It proposes checking whether the model can combine evidence, relate claims, and notice contradictions across distant passages.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main issue is that the context window tells you how much text you can put into the model, but it doesn’t tell you how effectively the model can use that text. Those are different things.

For example, finding a particular fact somewhere in a long document is a relatively simple task. You might give the model a very large amount of text, ask it to retrieve one detail, and find that it does quite well. But that doesn’t mean it can follow an argument spread across the whole document, reconcile different pieces of evidence, or notice that something near the end changes how it should interpret something near the beginning.

So I’d think of long-context ability as a collection of capabilities that you need to measure on the tasks you actually care about. The advertised window is a capacity limit. It isn’t a guarantee that the model’s performance will stay equally good as you fill it up.

r001.rationale: The response says performance is not guaranteed to stay equally good as the window fills, but does not clearly state that it can degrade substantially within the advertised limit.

r002.rationale: It describes retrieving a specific fact from a long document as a simple task and distinguishes that from broader long-context understanding.

r003.rationale: It does not propose measuring hallucinations about a supplied long document.

r004.rationale: It proposes assessing whether the model can follow arguments across the document, reconcile evidence, and use later text to reinterpret earlier text.
